scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: Class analysis and scientific socialism remain the right framework for understanding liberation struggles.
Imperialism should be analysed primarily as a stage and structure of capitalism, in Marxist terms.
A liberation movement's programme should be grounded in a materialist analysis of class and capital.
Socialism, understood in the Marxist sense, is the proper end goal of national liberation.
The vocabulary of scientific socialism translates well enough to describe any nation's path to liberation.
A liberation movement without a class analysis of its own society will misdiagnose its real obstacles.
The nation's own cultural and communal traditions, not imported Marxist theory, are the right foundation for its socialism.
A borrowed European framework like Marxism doesn't fit the specific history and social structure of this nation.
Indigenous values of community and solidarity are a sounder basis for socialism than imported class theory.
This nation's socialism has to be built from its own traditions, not translated from foreign doctrine.
Applying Marxist categories developed for industrial Europe to this society distorts more than it explains.
The nation's own precolonial traditions of communal life are a truer foundation for its politics than any imported ideology.
A disciplined vanguard party, once in power, should hold and use the state to build the new society.
Building strong state institutions is the necessary vehicle for consolidating national liberation.
The party-state is the legitimate instrument through which liberation is defended and carried forward.
A revolutionary government needs to control the commanding heights of the state to make liberation durable.
National liberation is secured through state power, not despite it.
A single leading party, coordinating through the state apparatus, is the right vehicle for this nation's revolution.
Autonomous communities and grassroots movements, not a party controlling the state, are where liberation actually lives.
The state, even a revolutionary one, tends to become a new structure of domination over the people it claims to liberate.
Liberation should be built from below, through self-governing communities, rather than delegated to a party-state.
A movement that hands its power to a centralised state has already compromised its liberatory character.
Autonomy and self-organisation at the local level matter more than capturing state power.
Real liberation resists being absorbed into any single party or state apparatus, revolutionary or not.
Political liberation should be pursued on explicitly secular grounds, separate from religious authority.
Religious institutions should not have formal influence over a liberation movement's politics.
A secular state is the right framework for uniting a diverse population around a common liberation project.
Mixing religious authority into liberation politics risks excluding those who don't share the majority faith.
The movement's legitimacy should rest on national and social grounds, not religious ones.
Keeping religion out of formal politics helps liberation movements stay unified across religious lines.
Religious faith and identity are integral to this people's liberation and shouldn't be set aside in the name of secularism.
A liberation movement that ignores the religious convictions of its people has cut itself off from real popular support.
Faith-based solidarity is a genuine and legitimate source of strength for a liberation struggle.
This nation's liberation is inseparable from the defence and revival of its religious tradition.
Religious leaders and institutions have a legitimate place in the leadership of a liberation movement.
A purely secular liberation project would betray what actually motivates and unites this people's struggle.
Liberation should focus on building this nation's own strength and self-reliance before anything wider.
A single nation's revolution has to be consolidated on its own terms before looking outward.
Overextending into regional or pan-national projects risks weakening what's been won at home.
Self-reliance within the nation's own borders is the soundest basis for lasting liberation.
This nation's specific struggle deserves priority over broader regional or pan-ideological ambitions.
A movement should secure its own house before committing resources to liberation elsewhere.
True liberation requires uniting with other peoples across the region into a broader union or federation.
This nation's struggle is inseparable from a wider regional or civilisational liberation project.
Artificial borders drawn by colonial powers should be transcended by a larger union of peoples.
Solidarity and unification across the whole region matters more than any single nation's separate path.
This nation's liberation is only a first step toward a broader union it should actively pursue.
Pan-regional unity is not a distraction from national liberation but its necessary completion.
Practical alliance with the Soviet bloc or its successors was, and remains, a reasonable strategic choice against imperialism.
Accepting military and economic support from a socialist power was a legitimate part of the liberation struggle.
Alignment with an anti-imperialist bloc strengthens a liberation movement more than strict neutrality does.
A liberation movement facing powerful enemies is right to seek powerful allies, socialist or otherwise.
Formal alliance with a socialist power doesn't compromise a liberation movement's independence in any meaningful way.
Turning down support from a sympathetic bloc out of a principle of non-alignment would have weakened the struggle.
A liberation movement should avoid dependence on any single foreign bloc, socialist or capitalist.
Strict non-alignment protects a movement's independence better than any alliance, however sympathetic, would.
Reliance on a foreign patron, even an anti-imperialist one, tends to compromise a movement's autonomy over time.
The movement's foreign policy should be judged case by case, aligned with no permanent bloc.
Non-alignment gives a liberation movement more genuine room to manoeuvre than any fixed alliance does.
Even a sympathetic foreign patron has its own interests that can come to override the movement's own.
Rapid state-led industrialisation is the surest route out of underdevelopment and dependency.
Heavy industry, built and coordinated by the state, is the backbone of real national development.
A five-year-plan style approach to industrial development is appropriate for a newly liberated nation.
Concentrating resources on industrial capacity, even at short-term cost, pays off in long-term sovereignty.
State-directed industrial development reduces dependency on former colonial powers faster than gradual growth would.
A strong industrial base is what ultimately secures a nation's independence, not just political sovereignty.
Development should build outward from self-sufficient rural and communal life, not from forced industrialisation.
Village-level self-sufficiency is a sounder development model for this nation than heavy industrial planning.
Rushing toward industrialisation risks uprooting the communal structures the nation's strength actually rests on.
A development model rooted in rural cooperation fits this nation's conditions better than an imported industrial model.
Strengthening local, communal production is more sustainable than concentrating on industrial mega-projects.
This nation's own agrarian and communal traditions offer a better development path than state-led industrialisation.
A single party, or a strong personalist leader, is necessary to hold the nation together through the liberation struggle and after it.
Multi-party competition, introduced too soon, risks fracturing a fragile post-liberation state along old colonial or ethnic lines.
Unified leadership under one party or leader is what has actually delivered liberation in practice.
The urgency of consolidating liberation justifies concentrating political authority for a time.
Factional political competition is a luxury a newly liberated nation often cannot yet afford.
A movement that fragments into competing parties too early tends to lose what it fought to win.
Multi-party democracy and open political competition should be established as soon as liberation is achieved.
Concentrating power in one party or leader, even temporarily, tends to become permanent and should be avoided.
Genuine liberation includes the right of the people to remove their own leaders through open competition.
A liberation movement should commit to pluralism as a core value, not a postponable luxury.
Political competition after liberation is a source of legitimacy and correction, not a threat to be managed.
Personalist or single-party rule, whatever its justification, tends to outlive the emergency that supposedly required it.
This nation's own workers and peasants, organised around their material interests, are the true agents of liberation.
Liberation has to serve the concrete interests of ordinary working people, not just national sovereignty in the abstract.
Class interest within the nation shapes who actually benefits from liberation and who leads it.
A liberation movement that ignores internal class inequality has left its work half done.
The struggle against internal exploitation is as central to liberation as the struggle against foreign domination.
Domestic elites who exploit their own people are as much an obstacle to liberation as any foreign power.
The nation as a whole, uniting across classes against a common external enemy, is the true agent of liberation.
Internal class conflict should be set aside while the more urgent struggle against imperialism is fought.
Liberation is first and foremost a national project, not a class one.
Emphasising class divisions within the nation weakens the unity liberation actually requires.
The colonising or imperial power, not any internal class, is the movement's primary target.
National unity against a common external enemy matters more right now than resolving internal class conflict.
